title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XL
paragraphs:
Wise in his daily work was he:
To fruits of diligence,
And not to faiths or polity,
He plied his utmost sense.
These perfect in their little parts,
Whose work is all their prize—
Without them how could laws, or arts,
Or towered cities rise?

To trace effects, even those of an electric battery, we often have to change position and examine a particular combination or group some distance from where the movement began. The group I am approaching sits at Caleb Garth’s breakfast table, in the large parlour with the maps and desk: father, mother and five children. Mary was at home for the moment, waiting for a job. Christy, the next child after her, was getting inexpensive education and inexpensive meals in Scotland. To his father’s disappointment he had chosen books over that sacred calling, “business.”

The post had arrived: nine expensive letters, for which the postman had been paid three shillings and twopence. Mr. Garth forgot his tea and toast as he read them and laid them open, one on top of another. Sometimes he slowly shook his head; sometimes he pursed his lips in silent argument. He did remember, though, to cut off a large red seal intact, and Letty seized it like an eager terrier.
The others talked freely around him. Nothing interrupted Caleb’s concentration except someone shaking the table while he was writing.

Two of the nine letters were Mary’s. She read them, handed them to her mother and sat absently playing with her teaspoon. Then, suddenly remembering it, she returned to the sewing she had kept in her lap throughout breakfast.
“Oh, don’t sew, Mary!” said Ben, pulling down her arm. “Make a peacock out of this bread for me.” He had been kneading a small lump ready for the purpose.

“No, you little mischief!” Mary answered cheerfully, giving his hand a light prick with her needle. “Try shaping it yourself. You’ve watched me often enough. I must finish this sewing. It’s for Rosamond Vincy: she’s getting married next week and can’t possibly marry without this handkerchief.” The last idea amused Mary, and she finished with a laugh.
“Why can’t she, Mary?” asked Letty, deeply interested in the mystery. She brought her head so close that Mary now pointed the threatening needle at her nose.
“Because it belongs to a set of twelve, and without it there would only be eleven,” Mary explained solemnly. Letty settled back, feeling she had learned something.
“Have you decided, my dear?” Mrs. Garth asked, putting the letters down.
“I’ll go to the school in York,” Mary said. “I’m better suited to teaching in a school than in a private family. I prefer classes. And I have to teach, you see; there’s nothing else available.”
“To me, teaching seems the most delightful work there is,” said Mrs. Garth, with a hint of reproach. “I could understand your objection if you didn’t know enough, Mary, or if you disliked children.”

“I suppose we never quite understand why someone dislikes what we enjoy, mother,” Mary answered rather shortly. “I’m not fond of classrooms. I prefer the world outside. It’s a very inconvenient fault of mine.”
“It must be terribly dull, always being in a girls’ school,” said Alfred. “All those idiots, like Mrs. Ballard’s pupils walking in pairs.”
“And none of their games are worth playing,” Jim added. “They can’t throw or jump. I’m not surprised Mary doesn’t like it.”
“What doesn’t Mary like, eh?” their father asked, looking over his spectacles and pausing before opening the next letter.
“Being surrounded by silly girls,” Alfred answered.
“Is it the job you heard about, Mary?” Caleb asked gently, looking at his daughter.
“Yes, father, at the school in York. I’ve decided to accept. It’s certainly the best offer. Thirty-five pounds a year, with extra for teaching the youngest piano strummers.”
“Poor child! I wish we could keep her here with us, Susan,” Caleb said, looking sorrowfully at his wife.
“Mary couldn’t be happy if she neglected her duty,” Mrs. Garth pronounced, conscious of having fulfilled her own.
“Doing such a nasty duty wouldn’t make me happy,” Alfred said. Mary and her father laughed silently, but Mrs. Garth replied with seriousness—
“Please find a better word than ‘nasty,’ my dear Alfred, for all the things you happen to dislike. And suppose the money Mary earns helps send you to Mr. Hanmer’s school?”
“I think that would be a great shame. But she’s a splendid old girl,” Alfred said, getting up and tilting Mary’s head back to kiss her.

Mary blushed and laughed, but could not hide her rising tears. Watching over his spectacles, his eyebrows drooping at the corners, Caleb looked both delighted and sad before returning to his letter. Even Mrs. Garth, whose lips curved in quiet satisfaction, let the unsuitable language go uncorrected. Ben immediately picked it up, singing, “She’s a splendid old girl, old girl, old girl!” to a galloping rhythm which he beat out with his fist on Mary’s arm.

Now Mrs. Garth’s attention shifted to her husband, who was already deeply absorbed in the letter he had just opened. His expression of serious surprise worried her a little. But he disliked being interrupted with questions while reading, so she continued to watch anxiously until a small, delighted laugh suddenly shook him. Turning back to the beginning of the letter, he looked at her over his spectacles and said in a low voice, “What do you think, Susan?”

She stood behind him and placed a hand on his shoulder while they read the letter together. Sir James Chettam was offering Mr. Garth the management of the family estates at Freshitt and elsewhere. He added that Mr. Brooke of Tipton had asked him to find out whether Mr. Garth would also be willing to resume managing the Tipton property. In very courteous terms, Sir James explained that he particularly wished to see Freshitt and Tipton under one management. He hoped to show that the two appointments could be combined on terms Mr. Garth would find agreeable, and would be pleased to see him at the Hall at noon the following day.

“That’s a generous letter, isn’t it, Susan?” Caleb said, looking up at his wife. She moved her hand from his shoulder to his ear and rested her chin on his head. “I can see Brooke didn’t like to ask me himself,” he went on, laughing silently.

“This is an honour for your father, children,” Mrs. Garth said, turning to the five pairs of eyes fixed on their parents. “The people who dismissed him years ago are asking him to return. It proves he did his work so well that they miss him.”
“Like Cincinnatus—hooray!” Ben cried, rocking astride his chair in comfortable confidence that the usual rules had been suspended.
“Will they come and fetch him, mother?” Letty asked, picturing the Mayor and Corporation in their ceremonial robes.
Mrs. Garth smiled and patted Letty’s head. But her husband was gathering his letters, about to retreat beyond reach into the sanctuary called “business.” She pressed his shoulder and spoke firmly—
“Now, Caleb, make sure you ask for proper pay.”

“Oh, certainly,” Caleb replied in a deep tone of agreement, as if no one could reasonably have expected otherwise. “Together they’ll bring in between four and five hundred.” Then he gave a small start of recollection. “Mary, write and turn down the school. Stay here and help your mother. Now I’ve thought of that, I’m as pleased as Punch.”

No one’s manner could have resembled the triumphant Punch less than Caleb’s. But finding phrases was not his talent, although he took great care over his letters and regarded his wife as a storehouse of correct expression.

The children were almost in uproar now. Mary held her cambric embroidery towards her mother, pleading for it to be rescued while the boys dragged her into a dance. Serenely happy, Mrs. Garth began collecting the cups and plates. Caleb pushed his chair back as though intending to go to his desk, but remained seated with his letters in his hand. He looked thoughtfully at the floor, stretching the fingers of his left hand in a silent language of his own. At last he spoke—

“It’s a terrible pity Christy didn’t take to business, Susan. I’ll need help before long. And Alfred must go off to engineering; I’ve settled that.” He returned for a moment to thought and gesturing fingers, then continued. “I’ll make Brooke draw up new agreements with the tenants, and I’ll work out a crop rotation. I’d wager we can make excellent bricks from the clay at Bott’s corner. I must investigate; it would cut the repair costs. It’s a wonderful piece of work, Susan! A man without a family would be happy to do it for nothing.”
“Take care you don’t,” said his wife, raising a warning finger.

“No, no. But once a man understands the nature of the work, it’s a wonderful opportunity: to put a piece of the country in good condition, as they say, guide people into farming properly, and carry out some sound planning and solid building that will benefit both the living and those who come after them. I’d rather have that than a fortune. I believe it’s the most honourable work there is.” Caleb put down his letters, slipped his fingers between his waistcoat buttons and sat upright. Then, slowly turning his head aside, he continued with awe in his voice. “It’s a great gift from God, Susan.”

“It is indeed, Caleb,” his wife answered with matching warmth. “And your children will be blessed to have had a father who did such work, whose good work lasts even when his name has been forgotten.” After that, she could say no more about his pay.

That evening Caleb sat quietly, tired from his day’s work, his notebook open on his knee. Mrs. Garth and Mary were sewing, and Letty sat in a corner whispering a conversation with her doll, when Mr. Farebrother came along the orchard path. With the clumps of grass and apple branches, he shared the bright August patches of light and shadow. We know he liked the Garths, his parishioners, and had thought Mary worth mentioning to Lydgate. He made full use of a clergyman’s privilege to ignore Middlemarch’s social distinctions, and always told his mother that Mrs. Garth was more of a lady than any married woman in town. Yet, you see, he spent his evenings at the Vincys’, where the lady of the house, though less of a lady, offered a brightly lit drawing room and whist. In those days, respect was not the sole basis of social life. Nevertheless, the Vicar sincerely respected the Garths, and the family found nothing surprising in his visit. Even so, he explained it while still shaking hands. “I’m here as a messenger, Mrs. Garth. I have something to tell you and Garth on Fred Vincy’s behalf. The truth is, poor fellow,” he continued, sitting down and turning his bright eyes on his three listeners, “he’s been confiding in me.”
Mary’s heart began beating faster. She wondered how much Fred had confided.
“We haven’t seen him for months,” Caleb said. “I couldn’t imagine what had become of the lad.”

“He’s been away visiting,” the Vicar explained. “Home had grown a little too uncomfortable, and Lydgate told his mother he wasn’t fit to start studying yet. But yesterday he came and poured out all his troubles. I’m very glad he did. I’ve watched him grow up since he was fourteen, and I’m so much at home in their house that the children feel like my own nephews and nieces. Still, it isn’t easy to advise him. He asked me to tell you he’s going away. He feels so wretched about owing you money and being unable to repay it that he can’t bear to come himself, even to say goodbye.”
“Tell him it doesn’t matter a farthing,” said Caleb, waving a hand. “We felt the pinch and got through it. And now I’m going to be as rich as a Jew.”
“By which he means,” Mrs. Garth explained, smiling at the Vicar, “we’ll have enough to bring up the boys properly and let Mary stay at home.”
“What treasure have you found?” Mr. Farebrother asked.

“I’m to manage two estates, Freshitt and Tipton, perhaps with a nice little piece of land at Lowick as well. They’re all connected by family, and once work starts flowing it spreads like water. It makes me very happy, Mr. Farebrother”—Caleb leaned his head back a little and spread his arms along the chair arms—“to have another chance at letting land and putting one or two ideas for improvements into practice. As I’ve often told Susan, it’s dreadfully frustrating to sit on horseback looking over a hedge at something done wrong, without being able to put your hand to it and make it right. I can’t imagine how people in politics bear it. Seeing a few hundred acres badly managed is enough to drive me nearly mad.”
Caleb rarely volunteered such a long speech. But happiness worked on him like mountain air: his eyes shone, and the words came easily.

“My warmest congratulations, Garth,” said the Vicar. “I couldn’t have better news to take Fred Vincy. He spoke a great deal about the harm he’d done by making you part with money you needed for other things—robbing you of it, he called it. I wish Fred weren’t such an idle fellow. He has some very good qualities, and his father treats him a little harshly.”
“Where is he going?” Mrs. Garth asked somewhat coldly.

“He intends to try for his degree again, and he’s going up before term to study. That was my advice. I’m not urging him into the Church; quite the opposite. But if he goes and works hard enough to pass, he’ll at least prove he has some determination and energy. He’s completely adrift and has no idea what else to do. This much will satisfy his father. Meanwhile, I’ve promised to try to reconcile Vincy to his son choosing a different career. Fred freely admits he isn’t suited to being a clergyman, and I’d do all I could to stop anyone taking the disastrous step of choosing the wrong profession. He repeated something you said, Miss Garth. Do you remember it?” Mr. Farebrother once called her “Mary,” but his tact now led him to show her greater respect precisely because, in Mrs. Vincy’s words, she worked for her bread.
Mary felt uneasy but determined to take it lightly. She answered at once, “I’ve said so many rude things to Fred. We’ve been playmates for so long.”
“According to him, you said he would be one of those absurd clergymen who make the whole profession look absurd. It was such a sharp remark that I felt a little of its edge myself.”
Caleb laughed with enjoyment. “She gets that tongue from you, Susan.”
“Not the flippant part, father,” Mary said quickly, afraid her mother might be offended. “It’s rather unfair of Fred to repeat my flippant remarks to Mr. Farebrother.”

“It certainly was a rash thing to say, my dear,” said Mrs. Garth, who regarded speaking ill of authority as a serious offence. “A ridiculous curate in the next parish wouldn’t make us value our own Vicar less.”

“Still, there’s something in her point,” said Caleb, unwilling to see Mary’s shrewdness dismissed. “One bad workman makes people distrust others in his trade. Things are connected,” he added, looking down and shifting his feet uncomfortably, feeling that he had more thoughts than words to express them.

“Certainly,” the Vicar said, amused. “When we behave contemptibly, we tune other people’s minds to contempt. I agree with Miss Garth, whether her view condemns me or not. As for Fred Vincy, though, fairness requires a little allowance. Old Featherstone helped spoil him by raising false expectations. There was something positively devilish in leaving him nothing in the end. But Fred has enough good taste not to dwell on it. What troubles him most is having offended you, Mrs. Garth. He thinks you’ll never have a good opinion of him again.”
“Fred has disappointed me,” Mrs. Garth said firmly. “But when he gives me good reason, I’ll be ready to think well of him again.”
At this point Mary left the room, taking little Letty along with her.

“Oh, we must forgive young people when they’re sorry,” Caleb said, watching Mary shut the door. “And you’re right, Mr. Farebrother, that old man had the devil in him. Now Mary’s out of the room, I must tell you something. Only Susan and I know, and you mustn’t repeat it. The old scoundrel wanted Mary to burn one of his wills the very night he died, when she was sitting up alone with him. He offered her some money from the box beside him if she’d do it. But Mary couldn’t possibly do such a thing, you understand. She wouldn’t touch his iron chest, or anything of that sort. Now, the will he wanted burnt was the latest one. If Mary had obeyed him, Fred Vincy would have received ten thousand pounds. The old man did turn back towards him at the very end. Poor Mary feels that deeply. She couldn’t help it, and she acted rightly, but she says it feels like knocking down someone’s property and accidentally breaking it while properly defending yourself. Somehow I feel it with her. Instead of holding a grudge for the harm the poor lad did us, I’d gladly make it up to him if I could. What do you think, sir? Susan disagrees. She says—tell him what you say, Susan.”
“Mary couldn’t have acted differently, even if she had known how it would affect Fred,” said Mrs. Garth, stopping her work and looking at Mr. Farebrother.
“And she knew nothing about it. I don’t think another person’s loss should burden our conscience when it results from our doing what is right.”

The Vicar did not answer at once. “It’s the feeling,” Caleb said. “The child feels that way, and I feel it with her. You don’t intend your horse to step on a dog when you’re backing out of someone’s way. But once it happens, it goes straight through you.”

“I’m sure Mrs. Garth would agree with that,” said Mr. Farebrother, who for some reason seemed more inclined to reflect than to talk. “I could hardly call the feeling you describe towards Fred wrong—or rather, mistaken. Though no man has the right to demand such a feeling from anyone.”
“Well, well,” Caleb said, “it’s a secret. You won’t tell Fred.”
“Of course not. But I will take him the other good news: that you can afford the loss he caused.”

Mr. Farebrother left soon afterwards. Seeing Mary and Letty in the orchard, he went over to say goodbye. They made a lovely picture in the western light, which brightened the apples on the old, sparsely leaved branches. Mary, wearing lavender gingham with black ribbons, held a basket; Letty, in her worn yellow cotton, gathered windfalls. If you want a more precise idea of Mary’s appearance, the odds are you will see a face like hers tomorrow in a crowded street, provided you watch for it. She will not be among those daughters of Zion who walk proudly, with necks stretched high, wandering eyes and mincing steps. Let them pass. Look instead for a small, plump, brownish young woman whose bearing is steady but quiet, who looks about her without imagining anyone is looking at her. If she has a broad face, a square forehead, distinct eyebrows and dark curly hair, with amusement in her eyes that her mouth keeps secret, while the rest of her features are quite unremarkable, take that ordinary but agreeable person as Mary Garth’s portrait. Make her smile and you would see perfect little teeth. Make her angry and she would keep her voice low, but probably say something as bitter as anything you had ever tasted. Show her kindness and she would remember it for ever. Mary admired the handsome little Vicar, with his keen face and carefully brushed, threadbare clothes, more than any man she had known. She had never heard him say anything foolish, although she knew he did unwise things. Perhaps foolish remarks offended her more than any of his imprudent actions. At any rate, it was striking that the Vicar’s actual failings as a clergyman never seemed to provoke the scorn and dislike she already felt for Fred Vincy’s imagined future failings in that role. Such inconsistencies, I imagine, occur in minds more mature than Mary Garth’s. We reserve our impartiality for abstract merit and fault, neither of which any of us has ever met. Can anyone guess which of these very different men called out her particular womanly tenderness: the one she was most ready to criticize, or the other?

“Do you have a message for your old playmate, Miss Garth?” the Vicar asked. He took a fragrant apple from the basket she offered and slipped it into his pocket. “Something to soften that severe verdict? I’m going directly to see him.”
“No,” Mary said, smiling and shaking her head. “If I said he wouldn’t be ridiculous as a clergyman, I would have to say he’d be worse than ridiculous. But I’m very glad he’s going away to work.”

“And I’m very glad _you_ aren’t going away to work. I’m sure my mother would be delighted if you came to visit her at the vicarage. You know how she enjoys talking to young people, and she has a great deal to tell about the past. You really would be doing her a kindness.”

“I’d love to, if I may,” Mary said. “Everything has become too happy all at once. I thought longing for home would always be part of my life. Without that grievance I feel rather empty. Perhaps it filled my mind in place of sense?”

“May I come too, Mary?” Letty whispered. She was a most inconvenient child, listening to everything. But Mr. Farebrother sent her into delight by pinching her chin and kissing her cheek, an event she later reported to both her parents.

Anyone watching the Vicar closely as he walked towards Lowick might have noticed him shrug twice. I think the few Englishmen who use that gesture are never of a heavy nature—or, for fear of some ponderous exception, hardly ever. Usually they have sensitive temperaments and considerable tolerance for people’s smaller faults, including their own. The Vicar was conducting an inward conversation. He told himself that Fred and Mary probably felt more for each other than the affection of childhood playmates. Then he asked in reply whether this young woman was not far too fine for that unformed young gentleman. His answer was the first shrug. Next he laughed at himself for apparently feeling jealous, as though he were in a position to marry. “Which,” he added, “as any balance sheet would plainly show, I am not.” That produced the second shrug.

What could two such different men see in this “brown patch,” as Mary called herself? Certainly her lack of beauty was not the attraction. And let all plain young women beware of society’s dangerous encouragement to put their trust in being plain. In our old nation, a human being is a marvellous whole, slowly formed through a long exchange of influences. Charm arises between two such wholes: the person who loves and the person who is loved.
Later, when he and his wife were alone, Caleb said, “Susan, guess what’s on my mind.”
“Crop rotation,” Mrs. Garth replied, smiling at him over her knitting, “or perhaps the back doors of the cottages at Tipton.”

“No,” Caleb said seriously. “I’m thinking I could be a great help to Fred Vincy. Christy’s gone, Alfred will soon be gone, and Jim won’t be ready to start work for another five years. I’ll need help. Fred could join me, learn how things work and assist me. If he gives up the idea of being a parson, it might turn him into a useful man. What do you think?”
“I think his family would object to that almost more than to any other honest occupation,” Mrs. Garth replied decisively.

“Why should I care if they object?” Caleb said, showing the firmness that came over him when he had settled an opinion. “The lad is an adult and must earn his living. He has enough sense and is quick enough. He likes being on the land, and I believe he could learn the work well if he applied himself.”

“But would he? His parents wanted to make a fine gentleman of him, and I think he feels much the same himself. They all consider us beneath them. And if you made the offer, I’m sure Mrs. Vincy would say we wanted to get Fred for Mary.”
“Life’s a sorry business if nonsense like that is to decide it,” Caleb said with disgust.
“Yes, but some kinds of pride are proper, Caleb.”

“To me it’s improper pride that lets foolish notions stop you doing something good. No kind of work,” Caleb said fervently, extending a hand and moving it up and down for emphasis, “could ever be done well if you listened to what fools say. You must know inside yourself that your plan is right, and then follow it.”

“I won’t oppose a plan once you’ve set your heart on it, Caleb,” Mrs. Garth said. She was a firm woman, but knew that on certain points her gentle husband was firmer still. “Even so, Fred seems definitely to be returning to college. Wouldn’t it be better to wait and see what he chooses afterwards? It’s hard to keep people at something against their will. And you aren’t quite certain yet about your own position, or how much help you’ll need.”

“Well, perhaps we should wait a little. But I’m fairly sure I’ll have enough work for two. I’ve always had my hands full of odds and ends, and new things are always coming along. Why, just yesterday—goodness, I don’t think I told you!—two different men approached me about the very same valuation. Rather odd. Who do you think they were?” Caleb took a pinch of snuff and held it between his fingers as though it formed part of his explanation. He liked a pinch when he remembered it, but usually forgot he had that pleasure available.
His wife lowered her knitting and gave him her attention.
“Well, that Rigg fellow—Rigg Featherstone—was one. But Bulstrode asked first, so I’ll be doing it for him. I can’t yet tell whether they’re arranging a mortgage or a sale.”
“Surely the man isn’t going to sell the land he’s only just inherited—the land he took the name for?” Mrs. Garth asked.

“The devil knows,” Caleb replied. He never referred knowledge of discreditable conduct to any higher authority than the devil. “But I do know Bulstrode has wanted to get hold of a fine piece of land for a long time. And land is hard to come by in this part of the country.”

Instead of taking his snuff, Caleb carefully scattered it. Then he added, “Things take curious turns. There’s this land everyone expected Fred to get, though apparently the old man never meant him to have a foot of it. Instead he left it to that illegitimate son he’d kept secret, expecting him to stay there and annoy everybody as thoroughly as he could have done himself if he’d managed to live. I say, wouldn’t it be curious if Bulstrode got it after all? The old man hated him and would never use his bank.”
“Why would the miserable creature hate a man he had nothing to do with?” Mrs. Garth asked.

“Pah! What’s the use of asking why such fellows do things? The human soul,” Caleb said, lowering his voice and gravely shaking his head as he always did with that phrase, “the human soul, once thoroughly rotten, will grow every kind of poisonous toadstool, and no eye can discover where the seed came from.”

It was one of Caleb’s peculiarities that, struggling to find words for his thoughts, he caught at fragments of language associated in his mind with particular attitudes or feelings. Whenever he felt awe, a suggestion of biblical language haunted him, although he could scarcely have produced an exact quotation.
